To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NDA is associated with anticorrelated intrinsic (DMN) and extrinsic (dorsal attention) networks and that it is also associated with a precuneus (PCUN) network.
NDA is associated with anticorrelation of intrinsic and extrinsic brain networks and with activation in a precuneus-based network.

NDA in Tibetan Buddhist meditation is correlated with anticorrelation of default mode and attentional control networks in the brain, whereas NDA with minimized content is correlated with activation of the precuneus.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the NDA experience, which has been cultivated for thousands of years, can be associated with a specific neural network and that this network is different from the networks that are associated with other types of meditation.

NDA involves a network of brain regions that are involved in the self, in social cognition, and in the integration of sensory, cognitive and emotional processes, but that these regions are activated in a different way during NDA, as compared to the activation patterns observed during dualistic experience.
NDA is associated with a deactivation of the extrinsic network, which includes the default mode network (DMN), and an activation of the intrinsic network.
The main takeaway from our work is that

NDA can be reliably induced and measured, and that it is associated with a specific pattern of anticorrelation between the default and the task-positive networks, which may be a neural signature of NDA.
NDA can be experienced and studied in a systematic way and that it can be used as a tool for investigating the neural correlates of nonduality in meditation.
NDA, as experienced in meditation, is a state of consciousness with unique features that are not captured by existing neurocognitive models of consciousness.
